Among records 11-50 assigned to each pair, 81 records were considered analysable by both reviewers and entered the inter-reviewer classification analysis; 87 records were rated analysable in RSv1 and entered the FTA added-value analyses. In the later final AI classification evaluation, 37 of the 50 allocated records were analysable and contributed 306 leaf nodes. All 60 RSv2 records had two saved reviewer responses and were included in the additional-public-information reassessment.

3.1. Inter-reviewer classification agreement in RSv1

The primary inter-reviewer classification analysis included 81 records and 731 jointly retained leaf nodes and used post-L1-reassessment labels. Pooled kappa was 0.503 (95% CI, 0.456 to 0.548) for detailed 22-category classification, 0.529 (95% CI, 0.478 to 0.576) for HFACS layer classification, and 0.775 (95% CI, 0.716 to 0.825) for binary HFACS/non-HFACS classification.

The analysis included 24 records and 219 leaf nodes for AB, 29 records and 250 leaf nodes for CD, and 28 records and 262 leaf nodes for EF. Detailed-category kappa was 0.628 (95% CI, 0.551 to 0.695), 0.402 (95% CI, 0.307 to 0.484), and 0.488 (95% CI, 0.409 to 0.560), respectively. Observed agreement, AC1, and pair-specific In sensitivity analyses, micro-F1 was 0.315 using all factors and 0.416 when restricted to HFACS-labelled factors. Under the main eligibility rule, micro-F1 was 0.148 with strict quotation matching and 0.511 with partial overlap (Supplementary Table S7).

Among matched factor pairs, baseline exact-set agreement on recorded classification labels, including indeterminate, was 20/37 (54.1%). All 37 matched pairs had one label per reviewer, giving pooled nominal kappa of 0.446. Both reviewers assigned an HFACS layer in 32 pairs; exact layer-set agreement was 25/32 (78.1%), with pooled nominal kappa of 0.639. Confidence intervals are reported in Supplementary Results.

Exploratory inter-reviewer micro-F1 for relationships between contributing factors was 0.291: 23 links matched among 74 and 84 eligible links recorded by the two reviewers, respectively (Supplementary Results).

All saved quotations could be located in the supplied narratives for the 248 reviewer-extracted factors and 110 RSv2 factors. Quotations came exclusively from the improvement-measure field for 70/248 reviewer-extracted factors (28.2%) and 35/110 RSv2 factors (31.8%). Median saved reviewer evaluation time was 4.84 minutes (interquartile range [IQR], 2.24 to 11.80).

In the baseline exploratory analysis, factor micro-F1 was 0.453 in 34 records where either reviewer reported unclear actor, role, or scope, and 0.371 in the other 26. Across 46 records with defined factor F1 and recorded time, Spearman's correlation between record-level factor F1 and mean recorded reviewer time was -0.001.

3.5. Reassessment with additional public information

All 120 reassessments were complete. Responses without uncertainty accounted for 45/120 (37.5%) before and 56/120 (46.7%) after reassessment; not-analysable responses accounted for 41/120 (34.2%) and 42/120 (35.0%), respectively (Figure 4). Nineteen responses moved to a more analysable state, seven to a less analysable state, and 94 retained their original rating.

Exact inter-reviewer analysability agreement was 31/60 records (51.7%) before and 26/60 (43.3%) after reassessment. Pooled linear weighted kappa was 0.386 (95% CI, 0.189 to 0.564) before reassessment and 0.203 (95% CI, -0.011 to 0.395) after reassessment. By pair, weighted kappa changed from 0.398 to 0.113 for AB, 0.348 to 0.245 for CD, and 0.400 to 0.388 for EF (Supplementary Table S9).

The response versions presented for reassessment contained 244 factors; four patient-condition-only factors in the independent-extraction versions were not present in this baseline (Supplementary Methods S7). Across 244 paired before-and-after assessments of existing factors by the same reviewer, recorded classification-label sets changed in 26 (10.7%). Six factors changed from a recorded classification to no classification (Supplementary Results, classification-change breakdown).

Among 32 matched factor pairs with HFACS layers assigned by both reviewers at both time points, exact interreviewer layer-set agreement changed from 25/32 (78.1%) to 21/32 (65.6%), whereas the proportion sharing at least one HFACS layer changed from 25/32 (78.1%) to 27/32 (84.4%). For the 26 matched factor pairs assigned a single layer by both reviewers at both time points, pooled nominal kappa remained 0.668 (Supplementary Table S10). Median reassessment activity time was 1.13 minutes (IQR, 0.46 to 2.97).

3.6. AI classification agreement in RSv2

AI classified all 110 RSv2 factor texts. Predictions matched at least one RSv2 label for 46/105 factors with any RSv2 label (43.8%) and 32/90 factors with at least one HFACS label in RSv2 (35.6%). Among 75 factors with a single HFACS label in RSv2, detailed-category agreement was 25/75 (33.3%), with kappa 0.240 (95% CI, 0.101 to 0.390); layer agreement was 40/75 (53.3%), with kappa 0.373 (95% CI, 0.208 to 0.555; Figure 3B).

4. Discussion

>Discussion

4.1. Principal findings

Our staged evaluations of public medical incident reports identified disagreement in factor extraction between reviewers and in HFACS classification both between reviewers and between AI predictions and the reference standards. Under the tested conditions, FTA did not establish added value over direct classification or factorfrequency ranking. In RSv1, neither AI model reached the detailed-category kappa target, and exploratory AI classification of RSv2 factors with a single HFACS label yielded a detailed-category kappa of 0.240. Reviewer factor extraction without AI-generated candidates also showed disagreement, and most RSv2 records were analysable with uncertainty or not analysable. Before and after reassessment with additional public information, responses without uncertainty accounted for 37.5% and 46.7%, exact inter-reviewer analysability agreement was 51.7% and 43.3%, and pooled linear weighted kappa was 0.386 and 0.203, respectively.

4.2. Interpretation and comparison with previous studies

Disagreement in factor extraction between reviewers indicates that the challenge extends beyond AI classification performance. Ebara et al. reported high inter-reviewer agreement in sentence-level P-mSHELL classification of public medication-related reports and good BERT classification performance for some categories [7]. They excluded 20 of 1,212 initially retrieved reports (1.7%) because they lacked backgroundfactor descriptions. After segmenting the background-factor field, they also excluded sentences with missing or unclear background information or descriptions of post-incident actions, retaining 5,058 sentences for classification [7]. In our RSv2 cohort, reviewers extracted specific factors without AI-generated candidates from reports selected without manual difficulty screening, and disagreement was observed at this stage. Smits et al. evaluated root-cause identification and classification separately, while Wang et al. evaluated model classification of expert-extracted factor statements, also distinguishing factor identification from classification [6, 13]. Thus, classification performance on prepared inputs does not establish whether the same contributing factors can be identified from collected reports. Our findings indicate the need to consider consistency in factor identification and the reporting information that supports it, alongside improvements in classification technology. This supports reporting-system designers and operators strengthening documentation support so that the circumstances and context needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships can be recorded.

Limited contextual detail may partly explain the assessment difficulties. Nuckols et al. identified insufficient narrative detail for specific classification of provider factors, and Cohen et al. highlighted limited contextual information for identifying supervisory and organisational factors [4, 17]. Our assessment difficulties are consistent with these observations, and Ebara et al.'s exclusion of sentences with unclear background information further highlights the importance of considering input conditions when interpreting classification performance [7]. Although ambiguous descriptions, extraction criteria and reviewer judgement remain possible explanations, processes for recording the circumstances and context needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships also warrant attention alongside analytical methods. Cohen et al.'s Systems Approach For Event Reporting (SAFER) programme demonstrated the feasibility and acceptability of training nurses to organise event narratives and background information using Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation (SBAR) and describe contributing factors using the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) model [18]. Such documentation support offers a practical example for reporting systems, but its contribution to agreement in factor extraction and classification requires evaluation.

4.3. Implications for reporting systems

Organisations that operate incident reporting systems or develop reporting guidance could strengthen reporting forms, guidance and reporter education to help reporters document the circumstances needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships. Rather than simply requesting more detail, such support could use examples and prompts to help reporters describe the sequence of events and the surrounding work-system conditions [18]. In the US railway sector, the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) funds the Confidential Close Call Reporting System (C3RS), with NASA receiving and analysing reports as an independent third party. The system uses reporting examples and guidance within reporting forms. When reports lack detail, NASA analysts contact reporters by telephone to obtain additional information, supported by standardised questions tailored to the event type [19]. Healthcare reporting systems could support documentation of the circumstances and context needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships through reporting examples, guidance within reporting forms and, where needed, follow-up with reporters. The purpose is to provide a clearer basis for interpreting contributing factors and relationships, not to require reporters to establish causation. The usefulness of this support should be evaluated in terms of its contribution to factor extraction and classification, rather than increases in narrative length.

These implications may also apply to reporting systems in other countries that combine structured fields with narratives. The combination of structured items and narrative descriptions in JCQHC reports is not unique to Japan. It is also used in the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Common Formats and Finland's HaiPro system [12, 20, 21]. The World Health Organization (WHO) Minimal Information Model for Patient Safety Incident Reporting and Learning Systems similarly combines standardised structured information with free-text incident descriptions to support comparison across countries [22]. In HaiPro, Holmström et al. found disagreement between local classifiers and a researcher assessing the same medication-error reports, with the researcher identifying more contributing factors [21]. Although they compared routine classifications with researcher reassessment, whereas we assessed agreement between paired reviewers using HFACS on public reports, both findings suggest that structured categories alone do not eliminate differences in narrative interpretation. Assessing agreement in identifying contributing factors from narratives is therefore relevant to similar reporting systems in other countries.

4.4. Limitations

There are several limitations. First, we did not compare public records with complete original hospital reports. Context omitted during public release could therefore be mistaken for information never recorded, overstating the contribution of the original information-collection process to assessment difficulties. Second, despite common written instructions, practice assessments and calibration, reviewers had no prior HFACS experience. If unfamiliarity contributed to disagreement, attributing that disagreement to report content could overstate the contribution of insufficient information. Third, access to AI-generated candidates and classifications during RSv1 construction may have increased AI-to-reference agreement through anchoring. AI-assisted factor matching in the RSv2 cohort was not independently verified by humans; missed matches could lower micro-F1 and overstate disagreement in factor extraction, whereas incorrect matches could raise micro-F1 and understate disagreement. The effects of anchoring and matching errors were not quantified; sensitivity analyses examined dependence on eligibility and matching criteria, not matching accuracy. Finally, rereading and exposure to RSv2 during reassessment could influence responses and inter-reviewer agreement independently of the additional public information, confounding interpretation of its effects. Factor sets were fixed, so potential effects on identifying new factors were not assessed. Overall, these limitations prevent identification of the original information-collection process as the main cause of the observed assessment difficulties.

4.5. Conclusions

In evaluations of public medical incident reports, reviewers disagreed on contributing-factor extraction, and neither AI model met the detailed-category kappa target for Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) classification against the first reviewer-consensus reference standard (RSv1). Difficulty discerning relevant circumstances and context from the available reports may have contributed to these assessment difficulties. Organisations that operate incident reporting systems or develop reporting guidance could strengthen reporting forms, guidance and reporter education to help reporters document the circumstances and context needed to interpret contributing factors and relationships. Among records 11-50 assigned to each pair, interreviewer classification included 81 records considered analysable by both reviewers; FTA added-value analyses included 87 records rated analysable in RSv1. The RSv2 cohort involved independent human factor extraction without AI-generated candidates in 60 new records, following a separate five-record pilot. The dashed path carries independent responses into public-information reassessment, not RSv2. 3.2. Added value of FTA

The FTA added-value analyses included 87 analysable RSv1 records. FTA-based structural rankings and factorfrequency rankings selected the same five categories; both achieved recall at five of 0.113 against improvementrelated reference categories. The FTA-minus-frequency difference in recall at five was 0.000 (95% CI, -0.411 to 0.128). The criteria for a positive lower confidence bound and a top five different from frequency were not met; the stability criterion was met, and no improvement-input leakage flags were detected (Supplementary Table S4). Corpus-wide analysis did not proceed.

In the subsequent FTA-versus-direct-classification comparison using the same 87 records, the paired differences (FTA minus direct classification) were 0.086 for record-averaged precision (95% CI, 0.021 to 0.152) and -0.123 for record-averaged recall (95% CI, -0.195 to -0.050). The all-category micro-F1 difference was 0.032 (95% CI, -0.024 to 0.086). For L3/L4, micro-F1 was 0.325 for FTA and 0.457 for direct classification, a difference of -0.132 (95% CI, -0.237 to -0.028; Figure 2; Supplementary Table S5). Sensitivity analyses are reported in Supplementary Table S6.

3.3. AI classification agreement in RSv1

The final AI classification evaluation included 37/50 analysable records (74.0%), contributing 306 leaf nodes. Detailed-category kappa was 0.427 (95% CI, 0.359 to 0.493) for the selected GPT-5.6 Sol model and 0.499 (95% CI, 0.445 to 0.551) for the secondary Kimi K2.6 evaluation. Neither estimate reached the kappa target of 0.6. Layer-level kappa was 0.437 for GPT-5.6 Sol and 0.514 for Kimi K2.6; binary kappa was 0.668 and 0.734, respectively (Table 1; Figure 3A). Detailed-category AC1 was 0.653 (95% CI, 0.576 to 0.720) and 0.676 (95% CI, 0.610 to 0.737), respectively; both point estimates exceeded the AC1 target of 0.6. Observed agreement and AC1 at all three classification levels, with their 95% confidence intervals, are reported in Supplementary Table S2.

3.4. Agreement in contributing-factor extraction and the RSv2 dataset

All 60 records in the RSv2 cohort had two saved reviewer responses, yielding 248 extracted factors; 176 were eligible under the HFACS-or-indeterminate rule.

RSv2 contained 110 factors across 60 records. Record-level analysability was without uncertainty in 15/60 records (25.0%), with uncertainty in 23/60 (38.3%), and not analysable in 22/60 (36.7%). Fifteen factors had multiple classification labels, including 10 spanning multiple HFACS layers; five had no classification label. Human-assigned factor-level resolution status was source-confirmed for 48 factors, rule-adjudicated for one, unresolved for two, and missing for 59/110 (53.6%; Supplementary Table S8). AI-assisted matching identified 37 eligible factor pairs, yielding micro-F1 of 0.420 (95% CI, 0.303 to 0.527; Table 2). Both reviewers extracted no eligible factors in 14/60 records (23.3%).

Figure 2.

Figure 2. FTA versus direct HFACS category prediction under matched input conditions. Points show paired differences (fault tree analysis [FTA] minus direct classification) and 95% record-bootstrap confidence intervals in 87 analysable RSv1 cohort records from records 11-50 within each reviewer pair (labelled Main in the figure). Both methods used Kimi K2.5 with the event description and background as inputs; improvement measures were excluded. The reference targets comprised the RSv1-derived report-level set (Section 2.4). Precision and recall are record-level means; micro-F1 pools category counts. Intervals used 10,000 recordcluster bootstrap resamples stratified by reviewer pair. This exploratory comparison followed assessment of the criteria for corpus-wide analysis and does not measure clinical benefit. L3, unsafe supervision; L4, organisational influences.

Figure 3.

Figure 3. AI classification agreement with RSv1 and RSv2. Points show Cohen's kappa and record-cluster bootstrap 95% confidence intervals stratified by reviewer pair. A: 306 leaves from 37 analysable RSv1 records (10,000 resamples); detailed and layer scoring included non-HFACS categories. GPT-5.6 Sol was primary and Kimi K2.6 secondary. B: AI classification of 75 fixed RSv2 factors with a single HFACS label (10,000 resamples); non-HFACS predictions were retained. Panel B is exploratory conditional classification, not end-toend extraction. Cohorts, units and label spaces differ between panels. AI, artificial intelligence; HFACS, Human Factors Analysis and Classification System; RS, reference standard.

Figure 4.

Figure4. Analysability before and after additional public information. Cells show counts and row percentages of paired reviewer assessments. The matrix compares each reviewer's rating before and after reassessment, comprising 120 paired assessments of 60 records by two reviewers per record. Green cells denote movement to a more analysable rating, grey cells an unchanged rating and rose cells a less analysable rating. Additional information included factual public fields and reporter-assigned cause judgements. Reassessment was sequential and non-blinded and could not isolate effects of metadata, rereading, prior exposure to RSv2 or reporter judgements. Rating changes do not establish correctness or improved inter-rater agreement.

Table 1 . AI classification agreement on 306 RSv1 leaf nodes

Both models were assessed on the same 37 analysable records and 306 leaves from the final 50-record set. Detailed classification included 19 HFACS categories and one combined non-HFACS category; layer classification included L1-L4 and non-HFACS. The Kimi evaluation was added after the selected model's final run. It did not replace the primary result.

Table 2 . Human factor-extraction agreement across 60 records in the RSv2 cohort

Each pair assessed 20 different records. Factors with HFACS or indeterminate labels were eligible. Semantic correspondence was AI-assisted and had not been confirmed by humans. Bootstrap intervals captured record sampling variability conditional on those correspondences, not their potential errors.
